summary.text: Writing \(\alpha=v_2(m)\) and \(c_p=v_2(p-1)\) for odd prime divisors \(p\mid m\), the proof uses \(v_2(\varphi(m))=\alpha-1+\sum c_p\) together with \(p\ge 2^{c_p}+1\), sharpened to \(p\ge3\cdot2^{c_p}+1\) unless equality makes \(p\) a Fermat prime; product bounds and \(\sum_{k<t}2^k=2^t-1\) then show that any qualifying \(m<2^{2^t+1}\) must be exactly the prime Fermat number \(F_t\). For \(t=33\), \(F_{33}\) supplies the required totient divisibility when prime, while \(2^{2^{33}+1}\) always supplies it, so the uniqueness result determines the minimum in either case.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(r)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^r\mid \varphi(m)\}.
\]
We prove, with
\[
N=2^{33},\qquad F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1=2^N+1,
\]
that
\[
A(N)=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{N+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]

The main point is the following general classification.

**Lemma.** Let \(t>0\), put \(n=2^t\), and suppose that \(m>0\) satisfies
\[
2^n\mid \varphi(m),\qquad m<2^{n+1}.
\]
Then
\[
m=F_t:=2^{2^t}+1=2^n+1,
\]
and \(F_t\) is prime.

We first establish the ingredients needed for this lemma.

For a nonzero integer \(x\), write \(v_2(x)\) for the exponent of \(2\) in \(x\). Let
\[
\alpha=v_2(m),
\]
and let \(P\) be the set of distinct odd prime divisors of \(m\). For each \(p\in P\), set
\[
c_p=v_2(p-1),
\qquad
s=\sum_{p\in P}c_p.
\]
The prime-factor formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p^e\parallel m}p^{e-1}(p-1).
\]
For an odd prime \(p\), the factor \(p^{e-1}\) is odd, so its contribution to the \(2\)-adic valuation is zero, while \(p-1\) contributes \(c_p\). The prime \(2\), when it occurs to exponent \(\alpha\geq1\), contributes \(\alpha-1\). Thus, using \(\alpha-1=0\) when \(\alpha=0\),
\[
v_2(\varphi(m))=(\alpha-1)+s.
\]
Consequently, the divisibility \(2^n\mid\varphi(m)\) implies
\[
n\leq (\alpha-1)+s. \tag{1}
\]
Also, if
\[
m=2^\alpha\prod_{p\in P}p^{e_p},
\]
then every \(e_p\geq1\), and hence
\[
m\geq 2^\alpha\prod_{p\in P}p. \tag{2}
\]

Every odd prime \(p\) can be written
\[
p-1=2^{c_p}q_p
\]
with \(q_p\) odd and positive. Therefore
\[
p=2^{c_p}q_p+1\geq 2^{c_p}+1. \tag{3}
\]
There are two possibilities. If \(q_p=1\), then
\[
p=2^{c_p}+1. \tag{4}
\]
If \(q_p\neq1\), then, because \(q_p\) is a positive odd integer, \(q_p\geq3\), and hence
\[
p\geq 3\cdot2^{c_p}+1. \tag{5}
\]

We will call a prime in the first class, satisfying (4), a minimal-type prime, and a prime in the second class a nonminimal-type prime.

We also need to identify the minimal-type primes. Suppose that an odd prime \(p\) satisfies
\[
p=2^c+1,
\qquad c=v_2(p-1)>0.
\]
Write \(c=2^kq\), where \(q\) is odd. If \(q>1\), set \(X=2^{2^k}\). Then
\[
p=X^q+1.
\]
Since \(q\) is odd, \(X+1\) divides \(X^q+1\). Moreover, when \(q>1\), one has
\[
1<X+1<X^q+1=p,
\]
contradicting the primality of \(p\). Thus \(q=1\), so \(c=2^k\), and
\[
p=2^{2^k}+1=F_k. \tag{6}
\]
Therefore every minimal-type odd prime is a Fermat number \(F_k\), and for that prime
\[
c_p=2^k. \tag{7}
\]

We next record the product estimates that will turn the valuation bound (1) into a lower bound for \(m\). For any nonempty finite family of nonnegative integers \(d_i\),
\[
\prod_i(2^{d_i}+1)\geq 2^{\sum_i d_i}+1. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, on expanding the product, the term obtained by choosing \(2^{d_i}\) from every factor is \(2^{\sum d_i}\), the term obtained by choosing \(1\) from every factor is \(1\), and all remaining terms are nonnegative. Similarly,
\[
\prod_i(3\cdot2^{d_i}+1)\geq 3\cdot2^{\sum_i d_i}+1. \tag{9}
\]
For a one-element family this is equality. For a family with at least two elements, the all-nonconstant term is
\(3^r2^{\sum d_i}\), where \(r\geq2\), and is in particular at least \(3\cdot2^{\sum d_i}\); again the all-constant term is \(1\).

More generally, partition a finite family into a minimal part \(I_F\) and a nonempty nonminimal part \(I_N\). Combining (8) and (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\prod_{i\in I_F}(2^{d_i}+1)
 \prod_{i\in I_N}(3\cdot2^{d_i}+1)\\
&\hspace{2cm}\geq
(2^{\sum_{I_F}d_i}+1)
(3\cdot2^{\sum_{I_N}d_i}+1)\\
&\hspace{2cm}\geq 3\cdot2^{\sum_{I_F}d_i+\sum_{I_N}d_i}+1. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(I_F\) is empty, (10) is just (9). This proves the mixed product estimate in every case.

We now prove the lemma. Partition \(P\) as
\[
P=P_F\sqcup P_N,
\]
where \(P_F\) consists of the minimal-type primes \(p=2^{c_p}+1\), and \(P_N\) consists of the nonminimal-type primes.

### Case 1: \(P_N\) is nonempty

By (4), (5), and the mixed product estimate (10),
\[
\prod_{p\in P}p\geq 3\cdot2^s+1.
\]
Using (2), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
m&\geq 2^\alpha(3\cdot2^s+1)\\
 &=3\cdot2^{\alpha+s}+2^\alpha. \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]

First suppose \(\alpha=0\). Then (1) says \(n\leq s\). Hence (11) gives
\[
m\geq3\cdot2^s+1\geq3\cdot2^n+1.
\]
But
\[
2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n<3\cdot2^n+1,
\]
so \(m>2^{n+1}\), contrary to the hypothesis.

Now suppose \(\alpha>0\). Then \((\alpha-1)+s=\alpha+s-1\), so (1) implies
\[
n+1\leq\alpha+s.
\]
Thus (11) yields
\[
m\geq3\cdot2^{n+1}+2^\alpha>2^{n+1},
\]
again a contradiction. Therefore Case 1 is impossible.

### Case 2: every odd prime divisor is of minimal type

Thus \(P_N\) is empty and \(P=P_F\).

If \(P\) is empty, then \(s=0\). Inequality (1) becomes
\[
n\leq\alpha-1.
\]
In particular \(\alpha\geq n+1\). From (2),
\[
m\geq2^\alpha\geq2^{n+1},
\]
contrary to \(m<2^{n+1}\). Hence \(P\) is nonempty.

By (6) and (7), for each \(p\in P\) there is an index \(k_p\) such that
\[
p=F_{k_p},\qquad c_p=2^{k_p}. \tag{12}
\]
Distinct primes in \(P\) have distinct indices, since the Fermat numbers \(F_k=2^{2^k}+1\) are strictly increasing.

We divide this case again according to whether one of these indices is at least \(t\).

#### Case 2a: some \(k_p\geq t\)

We first show that in fact \(k_p=t\). If \(k_p>t\), then \(k_p\geq t+1\), and monotonicity of the Fermat numbers gives
\[
p=F_{k_p}\geq F_{t+1}=2^{2^{t+1}}+1.
\]
Because \(t>0\), we have \(2^t>1\), and therefore
\[
2^t+1<2^{t+1}.
\]
Raising \(2\) to these exponents gives
\[
2^{2^t+1}<2^{2^{t+1}}<F_{t+1}.
\]
Since \(n=2^t\), this says
\[
2^{n+1}<F_{t+1}\leq p.
\]
But \(p\mid m\) and \(m>0\), so \(p\leq m<2^{n+1}\), a contradiction. Hence \(k_p=t\).

It follows that
\[
p=F_t=2^n+1.
\]
Since \(p\mid m\), write \(m=pu\) with \(u\geq1\). If \(u\geq2\), then
\[
m\geq2p=2(2^n+1)=2^{n+1}+2>2^{n+1},
\]
again impossible. Therefore \(u=1\), so
\[
m=p=F_t.
\]
The number \(p\) belongs to the prime-divisor set \(P\), so it is prime. Thus \(F_t\) is prime, as required.

#### Case 2b: every \(k_p<t\)

The indices \(k_p\) are distinct and lie in \(\{0,1,\ldots,t-1\}\). Therefore, by (12),
\[
s=\sum_{p\in P}c_p
 =\sum_{p\in P}2^{k_p}
 \leq\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}2^k
 =2^t-1=n-1. \tag{13}
\]
In particular, \(s<n\).

If \(\alpha=0\), inequality (1) would give \(n\leq s\), contradicting (13). Thus \(\alpha>0\), and (1) becomes
\[
n\leq\alpha+s-1,
\]
so
\[
n+1\leq\alpha+s. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(P\) is nonempty, (8) and (4) show that
\[
\prod_{p\in P}p
 =\prod_{p\in P}(2^{c_p}+1)
 \geq2^s+1.
\]
Using (2) and then (14),
\[
\begin{aligned}
m&\geq2^\alpha(2^s+1)\\
 &=2^{\alpha+s}+2^\alpha\\
 &\geq2^{n+1}+2^\alpha\\
 &>2^{n+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
contradicting the assumed upper bound. Case 2b is therefore impossible.

The only remaining possibility was Case 2a, where we proved that \(m=F_t\) and \(F_t\) is prime. This completes the proof of the lemma.

We now apply the lemma to the minimum defining \(A(N)\), where \(N=2^{33}\). First observe that the set over which the minimum is taken is nonempty. In fact, for every \(r\geq0\),
\[
\varphi(2^{r+1})=2^r,
\]
so \(2^r\mid\varphi(2^{r+1})\). Taking \(r=N\), the number
\[
B:=2^{N+1}

automatically satisfies \(2^N\mid\varphi(B)\). Hence
\[
A(N)\leq B. \tag{15}
\]

We now split according to the primality of \(F_{33}\).

### If \(F_{33}\) is prime

The standard formula \(\varphi(q)=q-1\) for a prime \(q\) gives
\[
\varphi(F_{33})=F_{33}-1=2^{2^{33}}=2^N.
\]
Thus \(2^N\mid\varphi(F_{33})\), so \(F_{33}\) is an admissible value in the definition of \(A(N)\).

Also,
\[
F_{33}=2^N+1<2\cdot2^N=2^{N+1}=B,
\]
because \(2^N>1\). Suppose that some admissible positive integer \(m\) were smaller than \(F_{33}\). Then
\[
m<F_{33}<B=2^{N+1}.
\]
Applying the lemma with \(t=33\) and \(n=2^{33}=N\), we would obtain
\[
m=F_{33},
\]
contradicting \(m<F_{33}\). Hence no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(F_{33}\). Since \(F_{33}\) itself is admissible,
\[
A(N)=F_{33}.
\]

### If \(F_{33}\) is not prime

The number \(B=2^{N+1}\) is admissible by (15). Suppose there were an admissible positive integer \(m<B\). Applying the lemma with \(t=33\) would imply both
\[
m=F_{33}
\]
and that \(F_{33}\) is prime. This contradicts the present assumption. Therefore no admissible positive integer is smaller than \(B\). Since \(B\) itself is admissible,
\[
A(N)=B=2^{N+1}.
\]

Combining the two cases and substituting \(N=2^{33}\), we conclude
\[
A(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
2^{2^{33}}+1=F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is exactly the claimed conditional value of the OEIS sequence term.
